result.summary: Nestor meets the wounded kings, and Agamemnon proposes launching the ships, but Ulysses rebukes him and Diomed urges them to rally the troops. Juno borrows Venus's girdle, enlists Sleep and seduces Jove on Ida, so Neptune can help the Achaeans. Ajax fells Hector with a stone and the Achaeans drive the Trojans back.

scenes.title: Nestor leaves Machaon's tent
scenes.summary: Nestor hears the din, takes his son's shield and goes out to see the rout, then meets the wounded kings.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean fleet and army are being overrun now that the wall has fallen.

scenes.title: Council of the wounded kings
scenes.summary: Agamemnon proposes launching the ships. Ulysses rebukes him and Diomed proposes that they go to the fight and urge on the others.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans risk destruction at the ships, and Agamemnon risks losing authority.

scenes.title: Neptune encourages the Achaeans
scenes.summary: Neptune, disguised as an old man, comforts Agamemnon and shouts a mighty war cry.

scenes.title: Juno borrows Venus's girdle
scenes.summary: Juno dresses, lies to Venus and gets her charm-filled girdle.
scenes.stakes: Juno risks Jove's anger if her deception is found out.

scenes.title: Juno persuades Sleep
scenes.summary: At Lemnos Juno recruits Sleep with the promise of Pasithea, and he recalls how Jove punished him over Hercules. They go to Ida.
scenes.stakes: Sleep fears Jove's wrath; Juno risks her scheme failing.

scenes.title: Jove beguiled on Ida
scenes.summary: Juno lies to Jove, who is overcome by desire and lists his past loves. They lie down under a golden cloud and he sleeps.
scenes.stakes: Jove's attention to the war and Juno's safety if found out.

scenes.title: Neptune rallies the Argives
scenes.summary: Sleep tells Neptune that Jove is asleep. Neptune urges the Achaeans to exchange armour and leads them into battle.
scenes.stakes: The ships and the Achaean army are at risk of destruction.

scenes.title: Ajax fells Hector
scenes.summary: Hector's spear fails to hurt Ajax, and Ajax knocks Hector down with a stone. Trojan princes carry him to the Xanthus, where he revives.
scenes.stakes: Hector's life, and Trojan hopes of burning the ships.

scenes.title: Achaeans rout the Trojans
scenes.summary: Heroes on both sides trade kills until the Trojans flee, with Ajax son of Oileus killing most.
scenes.stakes: Trojan warriors are killed and the Trojans' lives are at risk in flight.

alias_notes.explanation: The gods' name for the bird whose shape Sleep takes; men call it Cymindis.
Patronymic distinguishing him from the other Ajax.

notable_quotes.reason: Agamemnon's blunt preference for flight over death shows his despair.
Venus's girdle holding love, desire and flattery is the passage's famous image.
Vivid simile of an oak struck by lightning for Hector's fall.

analysis.text: Divine manipulation turns the war: Juno's deception of Jove and Neptune's help reverse the Achaeans' fortunes, showing human fate tied to the gods' quarrels.
Leadership under strain is tested as Agamemnon falters and Ulysses and Diomed hold the army together.

legacy.text: The Deception of Zeus (Jove) became a classic theme for later poets and artists, including paintings by Rubens and Ingres' depiction of Jupiter and Juno.

fun_facts.text: The girdle Venus lends Juno is called the cestus in later tradition.

language_notes.text: Hecamede is a captive woman serving Nestor; she tended the wounded Machaon in Book 11, mixing the posset drink.
Redoubtable means formidable, inspiring fear.
Danaans is a name for the Greeks, like Achaeans and Argives.
Vaunted means boasted. Ilius is another name for Troy.
Achilles is angry because Agamemnon took his prize Briseis, so he refuses to fight.
Gerene is Nestor's homeland association; 'knight' here means horseman or charioteer.
Mooring-stones were stones used as anchors, with ships held offshore by cables.
'Flying ruin' means fleeing from ruin; 'fly' here means flee, not take flight.
Tydeus died in the war of the Seven against Thebes, and was buried there.
Spleen was thought the seat of anger and ill temper.
"Kept no blind look-out" means Neptune had been watching carefully; he was not unaware of the Achaeans' plight.
Neptune and Juno are both children of Saturn and Rhaea, so he is her brother; he is her brother-in-law as brother of her husband Jove.
"Hoodwink" means to deceive; "enamoured" means filled with love or desire.
"Girded" means bound around the waist; "bosom" here means chest; "manifold devices" means many woven designs.
"Danaan" is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans; Venus favours the Trojans.
Jove imprisoned his father Saturn after overthrowing him. Oceanus and Tethys, ancient river-and-sea deities, are said here to have raised Juno.
"Bootless" means unsuccessful, without profit.
Pieria and Emathia are regions of northern Greece (Macedonia), on Juno's route from Olympus toward Lemnos.
"Compunction" means hesitation or scruple; Sleep would do this to any other god without misgiving.
Juno sent storms against Hercules as he sailed home from sacking Troy, driving him to Cos, while Jove slept.
Night is a primordial goddess, so powerful that even Jove would not offend her.
Swearing by the river Styx was the gods' most binding oath, which could not be broken.
"Soughed" means rustled or sighed, describing the sound of wind-like movement in the trees.
The bird has a divine name (Chalcis) and a human name (Cymindis), a Homeric motif of the gods' own language.
Juno has just prepared herself with Venus's charmed girdle to seduce Jove and distract him, so Neptune can help the Greeks unseen.
Oceanus and Tethys are primeval Titan deities, the river encircling the world and his consort. Juno was fostered by them while Saturn ruled.
Ixion's wife, Dia in later tradition, is not named here. Ixion was a mortal king, so this is one of Jove's mortal affairs.
"Daintily-ancled" is a Homeric epithet meaning with slender, pretty ankles.
"The daughter of Phoenix" is Europa in later myth; here she is simply unnamed, mother of Minos and Rhadamanthus.
"Whereon" means whereupon: at that moment. "Dew-bespangled" means studded with glittering dewdrops.
"Earth-encircling" and "lord of the earthquake" are Neptune's stock epithets, presenting him as god of the sea surrounding the land and of earthquakes.
"Danaans" is one of Homer's names for the Greeks, along with Achaeans and Argives; all refer to the same army.
"Beguiled" means deceived or charmed. Juno tricked Jove with seductive wiles so that he would fall asleep.
"In dudgeon" means in sulky resentment. Achilles is angry at Agamemnon and refuses to fight, staying by his ship.
"Sally forth" means to rush out boldly to attack.
"Wounded though they were" refers to the leaders Diomedes (son of Tydeus), Ulysses and Agamemnon, who were injured earlier and cannot fight.
Boreas is the north wind personified as a god; his blasts raise rough seas.
The two bands are the shield strap and sword belt crossing his chest; the spear hit where they overlapped, so it did no harm.
"Like a top" refers to a child's spinning toy; Hector whirls from the blow.
Brimstone is sulphur, whose smell was associated with lightning strikes.
"Bite the dust" means fall dead or defeated; here Hector is only stunned.
"Darts" here means light throwing spears, javelins.
Naiad: a nymph of freshwater springs, rivers and streams; Satnius's mother is a divine river-nymph.
Vaunted: boasted triumphantly over a fallen enemy.
The house of Hades is the underworld, realm of the dead; Polydamas jokes that the spear will be the man's walking staff there.
"Heaven counselled his destruction" means the gods willed Archelochus's death, so the spear's swerve to him was fated.
Bestrode: stood astride the fallen body to protect it, a standard battlefield action.
Argive: Homer's common name for Greeks, like Danaans and Achaeans; here used scornfully with "archers".
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) was god of luck, gain and herdsmen, so favouring a rich flock-master suits him.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is "lord of the earthquake"; earlier in this book he rallied the Greeks while Jove was distracted.
"The son of Atreus" here is Agamemnon, identified by his father's name, as often in Homer.

context_notes.text: Machaon is a Greek healer, son of Aesculapius, the god of medicine. He was wounded earlier and is resting in Nestor's tent.
Diomed (son of Tydeus), Ulysses and Agamemnon have all been wounded in the previous day's fighting.
The Greek ships were beached in rows along the bay, with the wall built behind the last row.
Diomed lists his grandfather's family to prove his noble birth before speaking as the youngest.
Neptune, god of the sea, favours the Greeks. Achilles is sulking at the ships, refusing to fight after his quarrel with Agamemnon.
Ida is the mountain near Troy from which Jove watches the war. He favours the Trojans, so Juno wants to distract him.
Vulcan is the divine smith, god of the forge, who made many marvellous objects for the gods.
Venus is goddess of love and desire, and she supports the Trojans, though she yields to Juno's authority.
Lemnos was the island of Vulcan's smiths; Thoas was its king, so Juno finds Sleep in a place linked to her son.
Sleep (Greek Hypnos) and Death are twin sons of Night in Greek myth.
The Graces were goddesses of charm and beauty; Pasithea, whose name suggests relaxation, is a fitting bride for Sleep.
The Titans were the older gods overthrown by Jove and imprisoned below the earth, so they witness oaths there.
Gargarus is the highest peak of Mount Ida, near Troy, from which Jove watches the war.
Their first union was secret, against their parents' wishes. Jove's desire now mirrors it.
Vulcan, god of the forge, is Juno's son. His craftsmanship supplies the locked, private chamber.
The sun sees everything in Greek myth, so hiding from it shows how thorough the cloud is.
Neptune favors the Greeks and opposes the Trojans. He has been helping them quietly because Jove had forbidden the gods to intervene.
Hector, Priam's son, is the Trojan champion. He has driven the Greeks back to their ships and threatens to burn them.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), god of the sea, is secretly helping the Greeks while Jove is not watching.
Ships were hauled onto the beach and propped with stones, so stones lay ready as missiles.
The Xanthus is the river near Troy, also called Scamander; Homer calls it the child of Jove.
Antenor was a respected Trojan elder who counselled returning Helen, so Archelochus's death touches an important family.
Acamas is a Trojan ally; his brother is Archelochus. Promachus is a Boeotian Greek.
Ajax son of Oileus, the Locrian Ajax, is a distinct hero from Ajax son of Telamon, and was famous as a fast runner.

literary_notes.text: Nestor's indecision is compared to a silent swell waiting for a wind to set its direction.
Agamemnon blames Jove, though his own quarrel with Achilles helped cause the Greeks' trouble.
Ulysses' blunt rebuke shows his stern resolve and willingness to confront even the supreme commander.
Diomed's modest yet confident opening shows a young man respectful of elders but sure of his worth.
Comparing Neptune's shout to ten thousand men shows his godlike power and heightens the effect on the Achaean army.
The oil's scent filling heaven and earth when merely shaken exaggerates its divine potency.
Juno calls her tale a lie in the narration, yet asks for charms to "make peace," when she really intends to deceive Jove.
Juno's smile while hiding her purpose shows her as cunning and pleased with her own trick.
Juno bribes Sleep with a luxurious gift, showing her cunning and readiness to manipulate others to deceive Jove.
Jove's rage is shown as gods hurled about the house and a threat to fling Sleep into the sea.
Sleep repeats Juno's offer almost word for word, stressing his eagerness while demanding the strongest oath.
"Sweet-singing" characterizes the bird in a stock descriptive phrase, as Sleep disguises himself.
Juno's lie about reconciling Oceanus and Tethys is plain to the reader, who knows she aims to deceive Jove.
Jove's list of lovers is a traditional epic catalogue; it shows his appetite while flattering Juno as the greatest.
The earth sprouts a bed of flowers for the divine pair, as if nature itself serves their union.
"Sire of all things" reminds us of Jove's supreme power just as sleep and love leave him helpless.
Sleep leaves at once, his task done, while Neptune's growing eagerness shows the god's readiness to defy Jove once the chance arises.
Neptune cites Achilles' absence as a reason for confidence, though the Greeks have been badly hurt by it.
Comparing the sword to lightning conveys its dazzling, deadly power and marks Neptune as a terrifying divine warrior.
Waves, forest fire and wind are stacked in a negative comparison to convey the enormous noise of the armies.
Hector's fall is compared to a lightning-struck oak, conveying his size, sudden ruin and the divine force behind the blow.
The ringing bronze armour gives a vivid sound image, showing he is stunned but his gear is intact.
Polydamas's grim joke about the spear as a staff mocks the dying man, showing the cruelty of battlefield boasting.
Ajax's sarcastic reply returns Polydamas's taunt and shows his fierce anger.
Comparing the severed head to a poppy-head makes the horror vivid and chills with its casual cruelty.
Addressing the Muses directly is the epic's invocation, marking a turning point and asking for divine knowledge.
Calling Ajax "fleet" recalls his stock trait and explains why he kills most of the fleeing Trojans.
